The Fed's announcement on what it plans to do regarding monetary policy was announced in October, but it is likely that a decision will be made before the end of 2016. The Federal Reserve Board has stated its intention to raise interest rates by 25 basis points between June and September. This is intended to boost lending and investment spending by consumers and businesses as well as provide financial stability for banks. It would also help prevent inflation from rising too quickly.
The timing of this announcement, however, may not be so important as to whether or not banks are forced out of business because they cannot meet their reserve requirements. Instead, most observers expect the increase in rates to prove beneficial since it could reduce demand for credit while at the same time stimulating economic growth.

Minutes of the Federal Open Market Committee
January 31, 2005

Summary of Economic Activity
In most sectors of economic activity in December and early January, there was little change from a year earlier. Consumer spending remained robust while business sales continued to expand moderately at a modest pace. Labor market conditions were stable for most wage categories but showed signs of tightening during the period. Wage increases, which typically lag behind price increases, appear to be increasing at a slower rate as firms' expectations increase on pay raises over time and workers are putting more effort into their resumes than they did last year, particularly among African Americans. Housing markets strengthened somewhat after showing declines in recent months. In addition, energy demand picked up slightly after showing weakness in previous quarters. Manufacturing activity softened again despite moderate gains in new orders; however, output growth was still very strong relative to its historical average. Agriculture is characterized by high crop prices that have resulted in record profits for many producers. The agriculture sector also has benefited from unusually good weather

The unemployment rate had declined over a year-ago period; although this was not reflected in housing starts or commercial construction activity, it suggested that demand for workers continued to expand. In addition, employment gains remained robust while hours worked fell modestly. Respondents expected these developments would continue through 2015, with further growth likely to be spurred by technological advances and labor market conditions improving in coming months. On balance, most participants judged that business investment spending should remain above current levels as long as economic fundamentals appeared to favor such an outcome.

Participants generally expressed concern about recent data on the pace of growth in U.S. nonfarm payroll employment. While several respondents noted mixed signals from indicators indicating that job creation slowed somewhat during the third quarter compared with earlier quarters, overall their assessments of potential future job gain rates did not suggest that the economy was growing more slowly than warranted for employers' financial reasons. Total retail sales increased moderately in April and May. Auto dealers reported moderate increases in inventory, but most dealers had difficulty finding buyers for their vehicles. Sales of residential equipment were flat to slightly down. Manufacturers said production continued at a robust pace, although some manufacturers are considering plans to halt new orders because of the current slowdown. Residential builders indicated that there has been little change in demand for homes since mid-April. Leasing activity was mixed across industries; contacts generally cited positive developments on rental side but noted concern about home inventories. Contacts noted that one area that showed considerable improvement is nonresidential leasing, particularly commercial space. Tourism remains strong while hospitality activities have slowed due largely to concerns over recent hurricanes. Hotel occupancy rates remained above average and room prices continue to increase. Travel and tourism related spending declined during the pandemic; however, hotel occupancy rates remain high, especially compared with pre-pandemic levels. Commercial real estate markets improved modestly from previous reports. Homebuilders reported slight improvements

What will the Fed do at its next meeting?
The Federal Reserve Board's decision on monetary policy is expected to be announced in late May, but it may change at a later date. A typical approach would have been for the Board of Governors (BoG) to raise interest rates during the intermeeting period and then begin the gradual easing that has led to very low levels of U.S. inflation over the past decade. In this scenario, there would also likely have been an increase in the federal funds rate. However, another possibility was to proceed with only modest increases, as some analysts have suggested that more accommodative measures could further moderate inflation pressures, without necessarily raising longer-term interest rates. To achieve this end, some policymakers are now suggesting that the BoG should engage in more aggressive asset purchases or other types of open market operations. This could include buying agency debt and mortgage-backed securities directly from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. Consumer Spending
The Federal Reserve has lowered its short-term interest rate 10 times in the last nine months, to a record low of zero. While that’s impressive (at least for now), it is not likely to affect consumer spending too much – unless there are other factors affecting consumers’ purchasing power.
A common assumption among those forecasting future economic growth or predicting recessions is that when people have less money available to spend, consumption will drop off. But while this may be true under normal circumstances, if an unexpected event reduces disposable income significantly over time, then we could see more than just temporary reduction in overall spending levels.
That said, let us briefly look at some underlying indicators which show that household financial situation remains relatively stable even with all these monetary policy moves by central banks around world:

Most contacts noted that economic activity had been growing slowly or declined since the last period but maintained expectations for growth to be moderate over coming quarters.

qwen_finetuned.consumer:
Consumer Spending
District consumer spending firms reported mixed results in recent weeks. While overall sales remained positive, retailers noted further improvement among apparel and home goods categories as well as some softening of holiday-related products that had been strong over the past few months.
In manufacturing, activity edged down slightly for District firms compared with a year ago but continued to be solid at most retail outlets.
Retail Sales
Overall retail reports were generally positive across all sectors from late August through early September. Large stores such as big-box chain discounters have seen little change since last quarter's report while specialty retail chains reportedly experienced a rise in traffic. Big box sellers expect sales growth to continue in coming quarters; however, many contactors indicated they are concerned about higher prices being passed on by manufacturers or store employees due to increased labor costs.
Apparel was another sector where contacts cited increases in foot traffic despite very tight margins. On balance, both men's and women's clothing departments fared better than other categories, according to our latest survey.

At its next meeting, the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) is expected to be guided by a report on economic activity from the Economic Policy Staff. Based on that information, as well as other relevant data, the FOMC anticipates continuing strong growth in U.S. economic activity over coming quarters. The Committee believes that maintaining current conditions for asset purchases would support additional gains in labor market indicators while allowing further progress toward maximum employment. In this context, an appropriate rate of asset purchases remains roughly unchanged.

Even with inflation running slightly below its longer-run objective, however, the Committee continues to anticipate that price pressures have recently declined sufficiently to make monetary policy less restrictive than otherwise desirable.
